title: Wang Yangming: Knowing Is Doing
objective: After this level you can explain Wang Yangming's claim that knowledge and action are one, and the bamboo he stared at for days trying to find its principle.
summary: Wang Yangming gave up hunting for principle in bamboo, found it in the mind, and taught that true knowing already includes acting; critics reply that weakness of will is real.

cards.headline: Can you know something is wrong and do it anyway?
cards.body: Most people would say yes, all the time. The Chinese philosopher Wang Yangming said no: if you don’t act on it, you don’t yet know it. His road there began with a week of staring at bamboo.

cards.headline: Seven days of bamboo
cards.body: Wang Yangming (1472 to 1529) was a Chinese statesman, general and Neo-Confucian philosopher. As a young man he tried the method of the orthodox Neo-Confucian Zhu Xi: investigate things to grasp their principle. His friend Qian stared at the bamboos in front of a pavilion and fell ill on the third day. Wang took over and fell ill on the seventh. No principle appeared.

cards.headline: Looking in the wrong place
cards.body: Years later, in exile in what is now Guizhou, Wang had a philosophical awakening in 1508. Searching outside yourself for moral truth, he decided, had it backwards. The principle is fully present in every person’s mind. The bamboo was never going to tell him.

cards.headline: Knowing is doing
cards.body: Hence his best-known doctrine, the unity of knowing and acting. “Those who ‘know’ but do not act simply do not yet know,” he said. Being able to say something filial doesn’t mean you know filial piety. He borrowed an image from the Great Learning: hating evil is like hating a hateful odor. Recognizing the smell and recoiling from it aren’t two steps.

cards.headline: Isn’t weakness of will real?
cards.body: Picture a student caught plagiarizing who says, “I knew it was wrong, but I wanted the easy grade.” Zhu Xi, like Aristotle, would take that at face value: weakness of will. Wang would say the student didn’t really know. Critics reply that recognizing something as attractive or repellent doesn’t always lead to action.

cards.headline: Wang Yangming: Knowing Is Doing: the big picture
learned: Wang’s week of bamboo found no principle
Moral principle is already in the mind
Critics: weakness of will is real

questions.prompt: What did Wang Yangming stare at for days, trying to find its principle?

options.label: A river
options.rationale: It was a plant by a pavilion.

options.label: A mountain
options.rationale: It was a plant by a pavilion.

options.label: The night sky
options.rationale: It was a plant by a pavilion.

questions.explanation: Following Zhu Xi’s method, Wang stared at the bamboos in front of a pavilion and fell ill on the seventh day.

questions.prompt: On Wang’s unity of knowing and acting, what is true of someone who says cheating is wrong but cheats anyway?

options.label: They know perfectly well but are weak-willed
They know more than people who don’t cheat
options.rationale: Knowing, for Wang, shows up in action.

options.label: They don’t yet truly know that cheating is wrong
They have investigated things too little
options.rationale: Wang gave up that outward method.

questions.explanation: For Wang, those who “know” but do not act simply do not yet know.

questions.prompt: Confucius in Level 6 couldn’t bear ritual without reverence. Which claim of Wang Yangming makes a similar point about empty form?

options.label: Saying filial words doesn’t mean you know filial piety
Principle is found by staring hard at things like bamboo
Rituals are empty and should all be abolished
Knowledge comes before action as a separate step

questions.explanation: Both insist the outward form isn’t enough: for Confucius, ritual needs reverence; for Wang, filial words without filial action aren’t knowledge.
